Holmes drew a folded paper from his pocket and spread it on the table. “A map of the Colony of Victoria,” he said. “I telegraphed Bristol for it last night.” He covered part of it with his hand. “What can you read?”
“ARAT,” I read out.
“And with this uncovered?” He lifted his hand.
“BALLARAT.”
“Exactly so. That was what the dying man said; his son heard only the final two syllables. He was trying to name his murderer: so-and-so of Ballarat.”
“That is remarkable!” I exclaimed.

“It is obvious. You see how much that narrowed our search. A grey garment was our third certainty, assuming the son's evidence was accurate. We had left vague speculation behind and reached a definite description: an Australian from Ballarat, wearing a grey cloak.”
“Certainly.”
“And someone familiar with the neighbourhood. One can reach the pool only through the farm or the estate, where a stranger could scarcely wander freely.”
“Quite true.”
“Next comes the expedition we made today. By examining the ground I obtained those small particulars about the criminal himself that I passed on to that imbecile Lestrade.”
“But how did you discover those particulars?”
“You know my approach: it rests on close attention to small things.”
“I understand that his stride would give you an approximate height, and that the prints could tell you about his boots.”
“Yes. They were unusual boots.”
“But how about the limp?”
“The right footprint was consistently fainter than the left: he put less weight on that leg. Why? Because it was lame, and he limped.”
“And why the left hand?”

“The injuries described by the surgeon at the inquest struck you yourself. The blow came from directly behind, yet landed on the left. How could that happen unless a left-handed man delivered it? He waited behind that tree while father and son talked. He even smoked there. I found cigar ash, which my special knowledge allowed me to identify as Indian. As you know, I have studied the subject and written a short monograph on the ash of 140 kinds of pipe, cigar, and cigarette tobacco. Having located the ash, I searched nearby and found the discarded end among the moss. It was an Indian cigar of the type rolled in Rotterdam.”
“What told you about the holder?”
“The end plainly had not been in his mouth, so he must have used one. The tip was cut, not bitten, but the cut was ragged. From that I deduced that he had used a blunt penknife.”

“Holmes,” I said, “you have enclosed this man in a net he cannot escape. You have saved an innocent life as surely as if you had cut the rope around his neck. I see where it all leads. The murderer is—”
“Mr. John Turner!” announced the waiter, opening our sitting-room door and showing in a visitor.

The man was a strange, imposing sight. His slow, limping walk and stooped shoulders suggested physical decay, yet his immense limbs and hard, craggy, deeply lined features spoke of exceptional strength, both bodily and in character. A tangled beard, grizzled hair, and prominent drooping eyebrows gave him an air of power and dignity. But his face was ashen, and a bluish tinge marked his lips and the edges of his nostrils. One glance told me that a chronic, fatal illness had him in its grip.
“Please take the sofa,” Holmes said gently. “Did you receive my note?”
“Yes. The lodge-keeper delivered it. You asked to meet me here so there would be no scandal.”
“I thought a visit to the Hall might set people talking.”
“Why did you want to see me?” Despair filled the tired eyes he turned on my friend, as though he already knew the answer.
“Yes,” Holmes said, replying to his expression rather than his question. “It is true. I know everything about McCarthy.”
The old man buried his face in his hands. “God help me!” he cried. “But I would never have let the young man suffer. I give you my word: if the Assizes went against him, I would have told the truth.”
“I am glad to hear you say that,” Holmes replied solemnly.
“I would have confessed already, but for my dear girl. It would break her heart—it will break it when she learns I am under arrest.”
“That may not be necessary,” Holmes said.
“What do you mean?”
“I have no official position. Your daughter, I understand, asked me to come, and I am acting for her. But young McCarthy must be cleared.”
“I am dying,” old Turner said. “I have suffered from diabetes for years. My doctor doubts I have a month left. But I would sooner die at home than in prison.”

Holmes moved to the table, taking a pen and placing a sheaf of paper before him. “Tell us the truth. I will write down the facts; you can sign the statement and Watson can witness it. Then, as a last resort, I can produce your confession to save young McCarthy. I promise to use it only if absolutely necessary.”

“That will do,” the old man replied. “I may not even live to see the Assizes, so it makes little difference to me. But I want to spare Alice the shock. Let me explain it all. It took a long time to happen, but it will not take long to tell.

“You never knew the dead man, McCarthy. He was the devil in human form, I assure you. May God keep you from the clutches of a man like him. For twenty years he had me in his grip and ruined my life. First I must explain how he gained that power.

“It began at the goldfields in the early 1860s. I was young, hot-blooded, reckless, willing to try anything. I fell in with bad company, started drinking, and had no luck with my mining claim. Then I took to the bush: in your terms, I became a highway robber. There were six of us. We lived wildly and freely, sometimes holding up a station, sometimes stopping wagons on their way to the diggings. I was called Black Jack of Ballarat, and the colony still remembers us as the Ballarat Gang.

“One day we ambushed a gold convoy travelling from Ballarat to Melbourne. There were six troopers and six of us, so the fight was close. Our first volley emptied four saddles, but three of our own men died before we secured the loot. I pressed my pistol to the wagon-driver's head. That driver was McCarthy. God knows I wish I had shot him there and then. Instead I spared him, though his wicked little eyes were fixed on my face as if to memorise every feature. We escaped with the gold, rich men, and reached England unsuspected. There I separated from my old companions and resolved to live quietly and respectably. This estate happened to be for sale, and I bought it. I tried to do some good with my money to make amends for the way I had acquired it. I married too. My wife died young, but left me my dear little Alice. Even as a baby, her tiny hand seemed to guide me towards goodness as nothing else ever had. In short, I made a fresh start and did all I could to atone for the past. Everything prospered until McCarthy got his hold on me.
“I was in London about an investment when I met him in Regent Street, with scarcely a coat on his back or boots on his feet.

“‘Here we are, Jack,’ he said, touching my arm. ‘We'll be like family to you. There are two of us, my boy and me, and we'll let you support us. If you don't—well, England is a fine, law-abiding country, and there's always a policeman within calling distance.’

“So they came down to the west country. I could not get rid of them. Ever since, they have lived rent-free on my best land. I had no rest, no peace, no chance to forget: wherever I turned, that sly, grinning face was at my elbow. It became worse as Alice grew older. He quickly realised that I feared her learning my history more than I feared the police. Whatever he demanded, he got. Land, money, houses—I gave him everything without argument, until he demanded the one thing I could not give: Alice.

“His boy had grown up, and so had my daughter. Everyone knew my health was poor. What a fine opportunity, he thought, for his son to inherit everything! But on that point I stood firm. His cursed blood would not mingle with mine. I had nothing against the boy personally, but his father's blood was in him, and that was enough. I refused. McCarthy threatened me. I dared him to do his worst. We agreed to discuss it beside the pool, halfway between our homes.

“When I arrived, he was talking to his son. I waited behind a tree and smoked a cigar until he should be alone. But listening to him brought everything dark and bitter in me to the surface. He was urging the boy to marry my daughter with no more consideration for her feelings than if she had been a slut off the streets. The thought that such a man controlled me and everything I loved drove me mad. Could I not break his hold? I was dying already, and desperate. My mind was clear and my limbs still fairly strong, but I knew my fate was settled. Yet my reputation and my daughter could both be saved if I silenced that filthy tongue. I did it, Mr. Holmes. I would do it again. However deeply I have sinned, I have endured a martyr's life to make amends. But I could not bear to see my girl caught in the same net that trapped me. I struck him down with no more remorse than I would have felt for a loathsome, venomous animal. His cry brought his son running back. By then I had reached the shelter of the trees, though I had to return for the cloak I dropped as I fled. Gentlemen, that is the truth of everything that happened.”
“Well, it is not my place to sit in judgement on you,” Holmes said as the old man signed the statement we had prepared. “I pray that we may never face such a temptation.”
“I pray the same, sir. What will you do now?”

“Given your health, nothing. You know yourself that you must soon answer for your actions before a higher court than the Assizes. I shall keep this confession. If McCarthy is convicted, I must use it. Otherwise no mortal eyes will ever see it, and your secret, whether you live or die, will remain safe with us.”

“Then farewell,” the old man said solemnly. “When your own deathbeds come, the thought of the peace you have brought to mine will make them easier.” His enormous body trembling and tottering, he slowly stumbled out.

After a long silence Holmes said, “God help us! Why does fate play these tricks on poor, helpless creatures? Whenever I hear a case like this, I remember Baxter's words and say, ‘There, but for the grace of God, goes Sherlock Holmes.’”

At the Assizes James McCarthy was acquitted, thanks to objections Holmes had prepared and passed to the defence counsel. Turner survived our meeting by seven months, but is now dead. There is every prospect that the young man and woman may come to live happily together, unaware of the dark shadow over their past.

chapters.title: The Five Orange Pips
paragraphs: Looking back through my notes and records of Sherlock Holmes's cases between 1882 and 1890, I encounter so many affairs with strange and interesting features that it is difficult to decide which I should tell and which I should leave aside. Some, however, have already become familiar to the public through newspaper reports. Others gave little scope for the particular abilities my friend possessed so abundantly, and which these accounts are intended to illustrate. Some defeated even his analytical powers and would make narratives with beginnings but no endings. Others were only partly solved, their explanations resting on conjecture and guesswork rather than the complete logical proof he valued so highly. One of that last group, however, was so extraordinary in its details and so startling in its consequences that I am tempted to describe it, despite certain aspects which have never been fully explained and probably never will be.

In 1887 we dealt with a long succession of cases of varying interest, whose records I still possess. The headings for that single year include the Paradol Chamber adventure; the Amateur Mendicant Society, which maintained a luxurious club in the lower vault of a furniture warehouse; the loss of the British barque _Sophy Anderson_; the remarkable adventures of the Grice Patersons on the island of Uffa; and the Camberwell poisoning. In that last affair, readers may remember, Holmes wound the dead man's watch and thereby proved it had been wound two hours earlier. The man must therefore have gone to bed within those two hours—a deduction crucial to solving the case. I may describe these affairs another time, but none is as peculiar as the chain of events I am now about to set down.

It was late September, and the equinoctial storms had arrived with unusual violence. All day wind screamed and rain struck the windows. Even at the centre of vast, man-built London, we were forced for a moment to look beyond life's routine and recognise the great forces of nature, roaring at humanity through the bars of civilisation like caged wild beasts. As evening fell the storm grew fiercer and louder, and the wind sobbed and wailed in the chimney like a child. Holmes sat gloomily on one side of the hearth, cross-referencing his crime records. Opposite him I was absorbed in one of Clark Russell's excellent sea stories, until the gale outside seemed part of the narrative and the rain's splashing merged into the long wash of waves. My wife was visiting her mother, so for a few days I was living once more in my old Baker Street rooms.
“Surely that was the bell,” I said, looking up at my friend. “Who would visit tonight? A friend of yours, perhaps?”
“Apart from you, I have no friends,” he replied. “I don't encourage callers.”
“A client, perhaps?”
“Then the case must be serious. Nothing less would bring anyone out in this weather at this hour. Still, I suspect it is more likely to be a friend of our landlady.”

His guess was wrong. A footstep sounded in the passage, followed by a knock. Holmes extended his long arm and turned the lamp away from himself, directing its light towards the empty chair intended for the visitor.
“Come in!” he called.

The visitor who entered was a young man, no more than twenty-two, neatly dressed and carefully groomed, with something refined and sensitive in his manner. The dripping umbrella in his hand and his long, glistening waterproof coat testified to the fierce weather through which he had travelled. Under the lamp's glare he looked anxiously around. I could see that his face was pale and his eyes heavy, as though some great worry weighed upon him.
“I must apologise,” he said, lifting a gold pince-nez to his eyes. “I hope I am not disturbing you. I am afraid I have carried some of the rain and storm into your comfortable room.”
“Let me have your coat and umbrella,” Holmes said. “We can hang them here to dry. I see you have travelled from the south-west.”
“Yes, from Horsham.”
“That mixture of clay and chalk on the toes of your boots is very distinctive.”
“I have come to ask your advice.”
“Advice is readily available.”
“And your help.”
“Help is not always so easy to provide.”
“I have heard of you, Mr. Holmes. Major Prendergast told me how you rescued him in the Tankerville Club scandal.”
“Ah yes. He was falsely accused of cheating at cards.”
“He said there was nothing you could not solve.”
“He went too far.”
“He said you are never defeated.”
“I have suffered four defeats: three at men's hands and one at a woman's.”
“But surely that is nothing beside all your successes?”
“It is true that I have usually succeeded.”
“Then perhaps you will succeed for me.”
“Please draw your chair up closer to the fire and give me some details about your case.”
“It is far from ordinary.”
“So are all the cases brought to me. I am the final court of appeal.”
“Yet I doubt whether even you, sir, in all your experience, have heard anything more mysterious or inexplicable than the events that have overtaken my family.”
“You have thoroughly interested me,” Holmes said. “Please give us the main facts from the beginning. Afterwards I can ask about whatever details seem most significant.”
The young man drew his chair closer and stretched his wet feet towards the flames.

“My name is John Openshaw,” he began, “but as far as I can understand, my own life has little connection with this terrible business. It is an inherited affair. To explain the facts, I must go back to its beginning.

“My grandfather had two sons: my uncle Elias and my father Joseph. Father owned a small Coventry factory, which he expanded when bicycling was invented. He held the patent for the Openshaw unbreakable tyre. The business prospered so much that he sold it and retired with a comfortable income.

“Uncle Elias went to America as a young man and established a plantation in Florida, where he apparently prospered. During the war he served in Jackson's army and later under Hood, rising to colonel. After Lee surrendered, he returned to his plantation for three or four years. Around 1869 or 1870 he came back to Europe and acquired a small estate near Horsham in Sussex. He had amassed a considerable fortune in the States. He left because of his aversion to the negroes and his opposition to the Republican policy of extending voting rights to them. He was peculiar: fierce, quick-tempered, extremely foul-mouthed when angry, and determinedly reclusive. I doubt he ever entered Horsham during all the years he lived nearby. His house had a garden and two or three surrounding fields, where he took his exercise. Often, though, he remained in his room for weeks. He drank large quantities of brandy and smoked heavily, but refused company and wanted no friends, not even his own brother.

“He did not object to my company; in fact, he grew fond of me. I was a boy of about twelve when he first met me. That was in 1878, when he had already spent eight or nine years in England. He begged Father to let me come and live with him and, in his own way, treated me very kindly. When he was sober, he enjoyed playing backgammon and draughts with me. He also appointed me to act on his behalf with both the servants and the tradespeople. By the time I reached sixteen, therefore, I was virtually master of the household. I held every key and could go wherever I chose and do whatever I pleased, provided I did not intrude on his privacy. There was one odd exception: a single storeroom among the attics, always kept locked, into which he would never allow me or anyone else to go. With a boy's curiosity I sometimes peered through its keyhole, but could see only the collection of old trunks and bundles one would expect in such a room.

“One morning in March 1883, a foreign-stamped letter lay before the colonel's breakfast plate. Letters rarely came for him: he paid bills in cash and had no friends. ‘From India!’ he said, picking it up. ‘Postmarked Pondicherry! What can this be?’ He tore it open. Five small, dried orange pips fell out, rattling onto his plate. I started to laugh, then stopped at the sight of his face. His lip sagged, his eyes bulged, and his skin turned the colour of putty. He stared at the envelope still held in his shaking hand. ‘K. K. K.!’ he screamed. Then: ‘My God, my God, my sins have caught up with me!’
“‘What is the matter, Uncle?’ I cried.

“‘Death,’ he answered. He left the table and went to his room, leaving me trembling with horror. I examined the envelope. Inside the flap, just above the gum, three K's had been scrawled in red ink. Apart from the five dried pips, it contained nothing. What could explain his overwhelming terror? I left breakfast and went upstairs. On the stairs I met him coming down with an old rusty key, presumably the attic key, in one hand, and a small brass box resembling a cashbox in the other.
“‘Let them do what they like; I'll checkmate them yet,’ he swore. ‘Tell Mary I want a fire in my room today, and send for Fordham, the Horsham solicitor.’

“I obeyed. When the solicitor arrived, I was asked to come upstairs to the room. A bright fire burned in the grate, among a mass of black, fluffy ash that looked like burnt paper. Beside it stood the brass box, open and empty. A glance at its lid startled me: there were the same three K's I had seen on the morning's envelope.

“‘John, I want you to witness my will,’ Uncle said. ‘I leave my property, with all its benefits and burdens, to my brother, your father. In due course it will doubtless pass to you. If you can enjoy it peacefully, well and good! If not, my boy, take my advice and give it to your worst enemy. I regret leaving you such a double-edged gift, but cannot tell which way events will turn. Sign where Mr. Fordham indicates.’

“I signed the paper as directed, and the solicitor took the document away with him. You can imagine how deeply that strange episode impressed me. I thought about it repeatedly, turning it over from every possible angle in my mind, yet could make nothing of it. I could not shake off the vague dread it left behind, although as the weeks passed without anything disrupting the usual routine of our lives, that feeling gradually weakened. My uncle, however, had changed. He drank more than ever and avoided company of every kind even more resolutely. Most of his time was spent in his room with the door locked from within. Sometimes a drunken frenzy seized him. He would burst out of the house and charge around the garden carrying a revolver, shouting that he feared no man, and neither man nor devil would pen him up like a sheep. Once the fit passed, he would rush back inside and lock and bolt the door behind him, like someone no longer able to defy the terror at the roots of his soul. At such moments I saw sweat shining on his face even on cold days, as though he had just lifted it from a basin of water.

“To conclude this part of the matter, Mr. Holmes, without trying your patience too far: one night he made one of those drunken excursions and never returned. When we went out to search for him, we found him face down in a small pool covered with green scum at the bottom of the garden. There were no signs of violence, and the water was only two feet deep. Given his known eccentricity, the jury pronounced it suicide. But I knew how he shrank from the very idea of death and found it difficult to persuade myself that he had deliberately sought it. Nevertheless, the affair passed. Father inherited the estate and about fourteen thousand pounds standing to my uncle's credit in the bank.”
“A moment,” Holmes interrupted. “I can already see that this is among the most remarkable accounts I have heard. What were the dates of your uncle's letter and his supposed suicide?”
“The letter came on March 10, 1883. He died seven weeks later, on the night of May 2nd.”
“Thank you. Please continue.”

“When Father took possession of the Horsham property, he made a thorough search, at my request, of the attic that had always been kept locked. We found the brass box there, though everything inside it had been destroyed. A paper label on the inside of its lid repeated the initials K. K. K., with the words 'Letters, memoranda, receipts, and a register' written underneath. Presumably these described the papers Colonel Openshaw had burnt. Otherwise the attic contained little of importance beyond numerous loose papers and notebooks concerning my uncle's life in America. Some dated from the war and showed that he had performed his duties well and earned a reputation as a brave soldier. Others dated from Reconstruction in the Southern states and mainly concerned politics. Evidently he had been very active in opposing the carpet-bag politicians who had been sent down from the North.

“Father moved to Horsham at the beginning of 1884. Everything went perfectly well until January 1885. On the fourth day after the new year, as we breakfasted together, he suddenly cried out in surprise. He held a newly opened envelope in one hand and five dried orange pips in the outstretched palm of his other hand. He had always laughed at what he called my cock-and-bull story about the colonel. Now that the same thing had happened to him, he looked frightened and bewildered.
“‘John, what on earth can this mean?’ he stammered.
“My heart felt like lead. ‘It is K. K. K.,’ I replied.
“He peered inside the envelope. ‘So it is!’ he exclaimed. ‘The very same letters. But what is written above them?’
“Looking over his shoulder, I read: ‘Put the papers on the sundial.’
“‘Which papers? Which sundial?’ he demanded.
“‘The sundial in the garden; we have no other,’ I said. ‘But they must mean the papers that were destroyed.’
“‘Nonsense!’ he said, making a determined effort to gather his courage. ‘This is a civilised country. We cannot allow such foolishness. Where was it sent from?’
“‘Dundee,’ I replied after checking the postmark.
“‘An absurd practical joke,’ he said. ‘What business have I with papers and sundials? I shall ignore the whole ridiculous thing.’
“‘I would certainly tell the police,’ I said.
“‘And let them laugh at me for my trouble? Certainly not.’
“‘Then may I go to them?’
“‘No. I forbid it. I won't have a commotion over such nonsense.’
“There was no point arguing; he was extremely stubborn. I went about my days with a heart full of foreboding, nevertheless.

“On the third day after the letter arrived, Father left home to visit an old friend, Major Freebody, who commands one of the forts on Portsdown Hill. I was glad to see him go: it seemed to me that he would be farther from danger while he was away from home. But in that I was mistaken. On his second day away, I received a telegram from the major, begging me to come immediately. Father had fallen into one of the deep chalk-pits so common in that district. He lay unconscious with his skull shattered. I hurried to him, but he died without ever regaining consciousness. Apparently he had been walking back from Fareham at dusk. Since he did not know the countryside and the chalk-pit had no fence, the jury had no hesitation in returning a verdict of death by accident. I examined every circumstance of his death carefully but could find nothing that suggested murder. There were no marks of violence, no footprints, no theft, and no reports of strangers seen along the roads. Nevertheless, as you can imagine, my mind was far from easy. I felt almost certain that some wicked plot had been woven around him.

“That was the sinister manner in which I inherited the property. You may ask why I did not sell it. Because I was convinced that our trouble arose from something in Uncle's past, and that moving to another house would leave the danger just as great.

“My poor father died in January 1885, two years and eight months ago. Since then I have lived happily at Horsham. I had begun to hope that the curse had left our family, ending with the previous generation. But I allowed myself to take comfort too soon. Yesterday morning it struck me in exactly the form in which it had struck Father.”
The young man drew a crumpled envelope from his waistcoat and shook five small, dried orange pips onto the table.
“Here is the envelope,” he continued. “The postmark is London, eastern division. Inside are precisely the words sent to Father: ‘K. K. K.’ and then ‘Put the papers on the sundial.’”
“What action have you taken?” Holmes asked.
“None.”
“None at all?”

“To be honest”—he hid his face in his slender, pale hands—“I have felt powerless, like a rabbit watching a snake approach. Some irresistible, relentless evil seems to have me in its grip. No amount of foresight or precaution seems capable of protecting me.”
“Tut, tut!” Holmes exclaimed. “You must take action, man, or you are doomed. Only vigorous action can save you. This is no moment to give way to despair.”
“I have spoken to the police.”
“Ah!”

“But they smiled as they listened. I am certain the inspector regards the letters as practical jokes and believes my relatives died accidentally, as the juries found. He sees no connection between their deaths and the warnings.”
Holmes waved his clenched fists. “Such incredible stupidity!” he cried.
“They have, however, provided a policeman to stay in the house with me.”
“Did that man accompany you tonight?”
“No. He was instructed to remain at the house.”
Once more Holmes made a furious gesture.
“What brought you to me?” he asked. “Above all, why did you not come immediately?”
“I didn't know. It was only today that I told Major Prendergast of my troubles, and he advised me to consult you.”
“You have had the letter for two days, then. We ought to have acted sooner. I suppose you have no evidence beyond what you have shown us—no further detail that might offer a clue?”

“There is one thing,” John Openshaw replied. Searching his coat pocket, he produced a discoloured sheet of blue-tinted paper and spread it on the table. “I vaguely remember noticing, on the day Uncle burnt the documents, that the small unburnt edges lying among the ashes were this particular colour. I found this single sheet on the floor of his room. I am inclined to think it may have fluttered out from among the other papers and escaped destruction that way. Apart from the reference to pips, I cannot see that it helps us very much. It looks to me like a page from some private diary. The handwriting is certainly Uncle's.”
Holmes shifted the lamp and we bent over the paper. Its ragged edge showed that it had indeed been torn from a book. Beneath the heading ‘March, 1869’ were these puzzling entries:
“4th. Hudson came. Same old platform.
“7th. Set the pips on McCauley, Paramore, and John Swain of St. Augustine.
“9th. McCauley cleared.
“10th. John Swain cleared.
“12th. Visited Paramore. All well.”
“Thank you!” Holmes said, folding the sheet and handing it back to our visitor. “Now you must not lose another moment. There is not even time to discuss your account. Go straight home and act.”
“What must I do?”

“There is only one course to take, and you must take it immediately. Put this sheet of paper you have shown us into the brass box you described. Add a note explaining that your uncle burnt all the other documents, and that this is the only one left. Make that statement in words that will convince them. Once you have done that, place the box on the sundial without delay, exactly as instructed. Do you understand?”
“Completely.”

“Put all thoughts of revenge aside for now. We may achieve that through the law, but our net still has to be woven; theirs is already in place. First we must remove the immediate danger threatening you. After that we can solve the mystery and punish those responsible.”
“Thank you,” he said, rising and putting on his overcoat. “You have given me new hope and a new hold on life. I will certainly follow your advice.”
“Do not waste a moment. And until then, take the utmost care of yourself. There can scarcely be any doubt that the danger is both real and immediate. How are you travelling back?”
“On the train from Waterloo.”
“It is not nine yet. The streets should be crowded, so I hope you will be safe. Nevertheless, you cannot be too careful.”
“I carry a weapon.”
“That is good. Tomorrow I will begin investigating your case.”
“Then shall I expect you at Horsham?”
“No. The answer to your mystery is in London. That is where I shall look.”

“Then I will return in a day or two and tell you about the box and papers. I will follow every detail of your advice.” He shook our hands and left. Outside, the wind still screamed and rain beat and splashed against the windows. The strange, savage story seemed to have emerged from the raging elements, blown towards us like seaweed in a gale, and now to have been swallowed by them again.

Sherlock Holmes sat silently for some time, his head lowered and his eyes fixed on the red glow of the fire. Then he lit his pipe and leaned back in his chair, watching blue smoke rings pursue one another upwards towards the ceiling.
“Watson,” he eventually remarked, “I believe none of our cases has been more extraordinary than this.”
“Except perhaps the Sign of Four.”
“Yes, perhaps that one. Even so, John Openshaw seems to be moving among dangers greater than those which threatened the Sholtos.”
“Have you reached any clear idea,” I asked, “of what those dangers actually are?”
“Their nature seems to me quite beyond doubt,” he answered.
“What are they, then? Who is K. K. K., and why is he pursuing this unfortunate family?”

Holmes shut his eyes, rested his elbows on the chair's arms, and brought his fingertips together. “The perfect reasoner,” he said, “given a single fact and a complete understanding of its connections, would be able to infer not only the entire sequence leading to it but every consequence that would follow. Cuvier could accurately describe a whole animal from one bone. Similarly, an observer who fully understands one incident in a sequence should be able to reconstruct all the others, before and after it. We have not yet fully understood how far reason alone can take us. A problem may be solved in a study after baffling everyone who has tried to solve it through direct observation. But to bring this art to its highest possible perfection, the reasoner must be able to use every fact he has ever learned. As you will appreciate, that implies knowing everything—still a rare accomplishment, even in an age of free education and encyclopaedias. Knowing everything likely to help in one's work is not so impossible, however, and that is what I have attempted. I remember that, early in our friendship, you once defined the limits of my knowledge very precisely.”

“Yes,” I replied, laughing. “A peculiar document. I remember putting philosophy, astronomy, and politics at zero. Botany, variable; geology, profound where mud-stains within fifty miles of London were concerned; chemistry, eccentric; anatomy, unsystematic; sensational literature and criminal records, unequalled. Violinist, boxer, swordsman, lawyer, and poisoner of himself with cocaine and tobacco. Those were the main findings, I believe.”

Holmes grinned at the last item. “I maintain now what I said then: a man should furnish his little mental attic with all the things he is likely to use. Everything else can go into the storeroom of his library, where he can fetch it if he needs it. For a case such as the one brought before us tonight, we must certainly call upon all our resources. Please pass me the K volume of the _American Encyclopædia_ from the shelf beside you. Thank you. Now let us examine the situation and see what conclusions we can draw from it. First, we can begin with a strong presumption that Colonel Openshaw had a compelling reason to leave America. Men of his age do not willingly abandon all their habits and exchange Florida's delightful climate for a lonely existence in an English provincial town. His extreme seclusion in England suggests fear of someone or something. As a working hypothesis, then, we may suppose that fear of someone or something drove him out of America. To determine what frightened him, we can only examine the ominous letters received by him and his successors. Did you notice the postmarks on those letters?”
“The first was Pondicherry, the second Dundee, and the third London.”
“East London. What conclusion does that suggest?”
“All are seaports. The writer must have been aboard a ship.”

“Excellent: we have already found our first clue. Certainly it is probable—highly probable—that the writer was on a ship. Consider something else. Seven weeks separated the Pondicherry warning from its fulfilment. At Dundee the interval was only three or four days. What does that suggest?”
“They had farther to travel.”
“But the letter also had farther to travel.”
“Then I fail to see your point.”

“At least it suggests that the man, or men, travelled in a sailing vessel. They seem to send their peculiar warning ahead when they begin their journey. Notice how quickly the deed followed the Dundee message. A steamer from Pondicherry would have brought them almost as soon as the letter. Instead there was a seven-week interval. I believe that interval measures the difference between the journey of the mail-boat carrying the warning and that of the sailing ship carrying its author.”
“That is certainly possible.”

“More than possible: probable. Now you see the deadly urgency and why I urged Openshaw to be careful. The attack has always followed after the time needed for the senders to complete their journey. This warning, however, was posted in London. We therefore cannot rely on any delay.”
“Good God!” I exclaimed. “What explains this merciless pursuit?”

“Clearly the papers Openshaw took with him are vitally important to the person or people aboard that sailing ship. I think it equally clear that more than one person must be involved. One man alone could not have arranged two deaths so skilfully that a coroner's jury was misled. Several men must have taken part, men of resource and determination. They intend to recover their papers, whoever may now possess them. Thus, you see, K. K. K. ceases to be one person's initials: it becomes the badge of a society.”
“But which organisation?”
Holmes leaned forward and lowered his voice. “Have you never—never heard of the Ku Klux Klan?”
“I have not.”
He turned the pages of the volume on his knee. Presently he said, “Here we are:

“‘Ku Klux Klan. A name derived from an imagined resemblance to the sound of cocking a rifle. Former Confederate soldiers founded this dreadful secret society in the Southern states after the Civil War. It rapidly established local branches across the country, particularly in Tennessee, Louisiana, the Carolinas, Georgia, and Florida. The organisation exercised its power politically, chiefly by terrorising negro voters and murdering or expelling those who opposed its views. Before committing an outrage, it generally sent its intended victim a warning in some unusual but recognised form: an oak-leaf sprig in certain districts, melon seeds or orange pips in others. The recipient could publicly renounce his previous conduct or flee the country. If he defied the threat, death invariably followed, generally in an unexpected and peculiar form. The society was so perfectly organised and its methods so systematic that scarcely any recorded case shows someone defying it without consequences, or an outrage being traced to its perpetrators. For several years it flourished despite opposition from the United States government and the better classes of Southern society. In 1869 the movement abruptly collapsed, although scattered outbreaks of similar activity have occurred since.’

“Notice,” Holmes said, putting down the book, “that the society suddenly broke up at the same time Openshaw left America carrying its papers. One may well have caused the other. It is no wonder, then, that some of its more unforgiving members pursued him and his family. That register and diary could implicate leading men throughout the South. Many of them may sleep uneasily until the documents are recovered.”
“Then the diary page we saw—”

“Was just what we should expect. If I remember, it said ‘sent the pips to A, B, and C’—that is, sent the society's warning. Later entries record that A and B cleared out, or left the country. Finally C received a visit, with, I fear, unpleasant consequences for C. Doctor, I think we can shed some light on this dark business. In the meantime, Openshaw's only chance, I believe, is to follow my instructions. We can say or do nothing further tonight. Hand me my violin, and let us spend half an hour forgetting the wretched weather and our fellow men's still more wretched behaviour.”
By morning the weather had cleared. The sun shone softly through the dim veil hanging over the city. When I came downstairs, Holmes was already eating breakfast.
“Forgive me for starting breakfast without waiting for you,” he said. “I foresee a very busy day ahead, investigating young Openshaw's case.”
“How will you begin?” I asked.
“A great deal depends on what my first enquiries reveal. I may have to visit Horsham after all.”
“You won't start there, then?”
“No, I will start in the City. Ring the bell, and the maid will bring your coffee.”
While waiting, I picked up the unopened newspaper and scanned it. A headline caught my eye and sent a chill through me.
“Holmes!” I cried. “You have come too late.”
“Ah!” He set down his cup. “I was afraid of that. How did they do it?” His voice was calm, but I could see how deeply he felt it.
“My eye caught Openshaw's name and the heading ‘Tragedy Near Waterloo Bridge’. This is the report:

“‘Between nine and ten last night, Police-Constable Cook of H Division, patrolling near Waterloo Bridge, heard a cry for help followed by a splash. The night was extremely dark and stormy. Despite assistance from several passers-by, rescue proved impossible. The alarm was raised, however, and with assistance from the river police the body was eventually recovered. It was that of a young gentleman identified, from an envelope in his pocket, as John Openshaw, a resident near Horsham. It is supposed he was hurrying to catch the final train from Waterloo Station. In his haste and the intense darkness, he apparently lost his way and stepped off one of the small landing stages used by river steamers. There were no signs of violence on the body. Undoubtedly this was an unfortunate accident, which should draw the authorities' attention to the state of the riverside landing stages.’”
For several minutes neither of us spoke. I had never seen Holmes so shaken or downcast.

“My pride is hurt, Watson,” he finally said. “A petty feeling, no doubt, but my pride is hurt. This is personal now. If God grants me health, I shall catch that gang. He came to me for protection, and I sent him away to die—!” He leaped from his chair and paced in uncontrollable agitation around the room, his sallow cheeks flushed, his long, thin hands nervously clenching and unclenching.

“Cunning devils!” he eventually exclaimed. “How did they lure him there? The Embankment is not on the direct route to the station. Even on such a night the bridge was probably too crowded for them. Well, Watson, we shall see who wins in the end. I am going out!”
“To see the police?”
“No. I shall act as my own police. Once I have woven the web, they may collect the flies—not before.”

My medical work occupied the whole day, and it was late evening before I returned to Baker Street. Holmes was still out. He arrived at nearly ten, pale and exhausted. Going straight to the sideboard, he tore a piece from the loaf and ate it ravenously, washing it down with a long drink of water.
“You must be hungry,” I remarked.
“Famished. I had completely forgotten. I have eaten nothing since breakfast.”
“Nothing at all?”
“Not a mouthful. There was no time to consider it.”
“And what success have you had?”
“Good success.”
“Have you found a clue?”
“I have them in my grasp. Young Openshaw will not go unavenged for long. Watson, let us send them their own diabolical calling card! An excellent idea!”
“What are you proposing?”

He took an orange from the cupboard, tore it apart, and squeezed its seeds onto the table. Selecting five, he put them in an envelope. Inside the flap he wrote ‘S. H. for J. O.’ He sealed it and addressed it: ‘Captain James Calhoun, Barque _Lone Star_, Savannah, Georgia.’
“It will be waiting when he reaches port,” he said with a chuckle. “Perhaps it will cost him a night's sleep. He will find it as certain a warning of his fate as Openshaw did.”
“Who exactly is Captain Calhoun?”
“The gang's leader. I will catch the others too, but him first.”
“How did you follow the trail?”
He produced a large sheet of paper covered in names and dates.

“I spent all day examining Lloyd's registers and old newspapers,” he said, “tracing the later movements of every ship that called at Pondicherry during January and February 1883. Thirty-six vessels of substantial tonnage were reported there in those months. One immediately stood out: the _Lone Star_. Although listed as sailing from London, it bore a name associated with one of the American states.”
“Texas, I believe.”
“I wasn't sure which state, and am still not sure. But I knew the vessel must be American in origin.”
“What did you do next?”

“I examined Dundee's records. Finding the barque _Lone Star_ there in January 1885 turned suspicion into certainty. After that I made enquiries about which vessels were currently in the port of London.”
“And then?”

“The _Lone Star_ arrived last week. At Albert Dock I discovered that she had gone downriver on this morning's early tide, homeward bound for Savannah. I telegraphed Gravesend and learned that she had already passed some time earlier. With this easterly wind, I have no doubt she is beyond the Goodwins by now and approaching the Isle of Wight.”
“What do you intend to do?”

“Oh, I have him in my grasp. I have learned that he and his two mates are the ship's only native-born Americans; the rest are Finns and Germans. I also know all three were away from the vessel last night. The stevedore loading their cargo told me. Before their sailing ship reaches Savannah, a mail-boat will deliver this letter. A cable will also inform Savannah's police that those three gentlemen are urgently wanted here on a murder charge.”

Yet even the best human plans contain a flaw. John Openshaw's murderers never received the orange pips that would have warned them they were being pursued by someone as resourceful and determined as themselves. That year's equinoctial gales were exceptionally severe and prolonged. We waited a long time for news of Savannah's _Lone Star_, but none came. Eventually we heard that, far out in the Atlantic, a shattered boat's stern-post had been seen tossing in a wave's trough, the letters ‘L. S.’ carved into it. That is all we shall ever know of the _Lone Star_'s fate.

chapters.title: The Man with the Twisted Lip
paragraphs: Isa Whitney, brother of the late Elias Whitney, D.D., Principal of the Theological College of St. George’s, was deeply addicted to opium. As I understand it, the habit began with a foolish experiment during his college days. After reading De Quincey’s account of his dreams and sensations, he soaked his tobacco in laudanum, hoping to produce the same effects. He discovered, as so many others have, that the practice is easier to acquire than to abandon. For years he remained a slave to the drug, inspiring both horror and pity in his friends and relations. I can picture him still: his yellow, pasty face, his drooping eyelids and pin-point pupils, his body huddled in a chair—the ruined remains of a noble man.

One night in June 1889, our doorbell rang at about the hour when a man begins to yawn and look at the clock. I straightened up in my chair. My wife lowered her needlework into her lap, with a little expression of disappointment.
“A patient!” she said. “You will have to go out.”
I groaned; I had only just returned after an exhausting day.
We heard the front door open, a few hurried words, then quick footsteps on the linoleum. The door of our room flew open, and a woman in a dark dress and black veil came in.

“Please forgive me for calling so late,” she began. Then, suddenly losing command of herself, she hurried forward, put her arms around my wife’s neck, and sobbed on her shoulder. “Oh, I’m in such trouble!” she cried. “I need a little help so badly.”
“Why, it is Kate Whitney!” my wife said, lifting her veil. “How you startled me, Kate! When you came in, I had no idea who you were.”
“I did not know what to do, so I came directly to you.” It was always like that. People in distress came to my wife as birds come to a lighthouse.
“It was very kind of you to come. Now have some wine and water, sit comfortably here, and tell us everything. Or would you prefer me to send James off to bed?”
“Oh, no, no! I need the doctor’s advice and help as well. It is about Isa. He has not come home for two days. I am so afraid for him!”

She had spoken to us before about her husband’s troubles—to me as a doctor, and to my wife as an old friend from school. We did our best to soothe and comfort her. Did she know where he was? Could we perhaps bring him home to her?

Apparently we could. She had reliable information that lately, when the craving seized him, he had been visiting an opium den at the far eastern end of the City. Until now, these bouts had lasted only a day, and he had returned in the evening, twitching and exhausted. This time, however, the spell had held him for forty-eight hours. No doubt he was lying there among the dregs of the docks, inhaling the poison or sleeping off its effects. She was certain we would find him at the Bar of Gold in Upper Swandam Lane. But what could she do? How could a young, timid woman enter such a place and drag her husband away from the ruffians surrounding him?

That was the situation, and naturally there was only one answer. Could I not accompany her there? Then another thought occurred to me: why should she go at all? As Isa Whitney’s medical adviser, I had some influence over him and could manage better alone. I gave her my word that, if he really was at the address she had supplied, I would send him home in a cab within two hours. Ten minutes later I had left my armchair and cheerful sitting-room behind and was travelling east in a hansom. It seemed a strange errand at the time, though only what followed could reveal how strange it would become.

The first stage of my adventure, however, presented little difficulty. Upper Swandam Lane is a filthy alley hidden behind the high wharves on the north bank of the river, east of London Bridge. Between a cheap clothing shop and a gin-shop, a steep staircase descended to a dark opening like the mouth of a cave. There I found the den I wanted. I told the cabman to wait and went down the steps, their centres worn hollow by the endless tread of drunken feet. By a flickering oil lamp above the door, I located the latch and entered a long, low room. Brown opium smoke hung thick and heavy in it, and rows of wooden sleeping berths rose in tiers like those in the forecastle of an emigrant ship.

In the gloom I could just make out bodies sprawled in bizarre positions: hunched shoulders, drawn-up knees, heads tilted back, chins pointing upwards. Here and there a dark, dull eye turned towards the newcomer. Small red circles glimmered from the black shadows, brightening and fading as the poisonous substance burned in the bowls of metal pipes. Most of the occupants were silent. Some muttered to themselves; others conversed in strange, low, monotonous tones, their talk spilling out in bursts before suddenly falling silent. Each mumbled his own thoughts with little attention to his neighbour’s words. At the far end stood a small brazier of burning charcoal. Beside it, on a three-legged wooden stool, sat a tall, thin old man, his jaw resting on his two fists and his elbows on his knees, staring into the fire.
As I came in, a sallow Malay attendant hurried towards me with a pipe and a supply of opium, gesturing towards an empty berth.
“Thank you, but I do not intend to stay,” I said. “A friend of mine is here, Mr. Isa Whitney, and I want to speak to him.”
Someone moved and exclaimed on my right. Peering into the darkness, I saw Whitney staring at me, pale, haggard, and dishevelled.
“My God! It’s Watson,” he said. He was suffering a miserable reaction to the drug, every nerve trembling. “Tell me, Watson, what time is it?”
“Almost eleven.”
“On what day?”
“Friday, the nineteenth of June.”
“Good heavens! I thought it was Wednesday. It is Wednesday. Why do you want to frighten a fellow?” He buried his face in his arms and began sobbing in a high-pitched voice.
“I assure you it is Friday. Your wife has been waiting two days for you. You ought to be ashamed of yourself!”

“I am. But you are mistaken, Watson. I have only been here a few hours—three pipes, four pipes, I cannot remember how many. Still, I will come home with you. I would not frighten Kate, poor little Kate. Give me your hand! Have you brought a cab?”
“Yes, there is one waiting outside.”
“Then I will take it. But I must owe them something. Find out how much, Watson. I feel terribly unwell. I cannot do anything for myself.”

I walked along the narrow aisle between the two rows of sleepers, holding my breath against the drug’s foul, stupefying fumes and looking for the manager. As I passed the tall man beside the brazier, I felt a sudden tug at the skirt of my coat. A quiet voice whispered, “Walk past me, then look back.” I heard the words distinctly. I glanced down. They could only have come from the old man beside me, yet he sat apparently as absorbed as before: thin, deeply wrinkled, and stooping with age. An opium pipe hung between his knees, as though exhaustion had made him let it slip from his fingers. I took two steps and turned. Only the greatest effort kept me from crying out in astonishment. He had turned his back on the room so that only I could see him. His body had filled out, his wrinkles had vanished, and his dull eyes had recovered their fire. There, beside the brazier, grinning at my amazement, sat Sherlock Holmes himself. With a slight movement he beckoned me closer. Then, as he half turned towards the room again, he instantly became a doddering old man with slack lips.
“Holmes!” I whispered. “What on earth brings you to this den?”
“Keep your voice as low as possible,” he replied. “My hearing is excellent. If you would kindly dispose of that drunken friend of yours, I should be very glad of a little conversation with you.”
“There is a cab outside.”

“Then please send him home in it. You can safely leave him to himself: he seems too feeble to get into trouble. I suggest you also give the driver a note for your wife, explaining that you have joined forces with me. Wait outside, and I will meet you in five minutes.”

Refusing Sherlock Holmes was difficult. His requests were always so precise, and delivered with such quiet authority. Still, once Whitney was safely inside the cab, my errand would be practically complete. As for what followed, I could wish for nothing better than to join my friend in one of those extraordinary adventures which formed the ordinary pattern of his life. Within a few minutes I had written my note, settled Whitney’s bill, taken him out to the cab, and watched it carry him away into the darkness. Soon afterwards a decrepit figure emerged from the opium den, and I found myself walking down the street beside Sherlock Holmes. For two streets he shuffled along, back bent and steps uncertain. Then he glanced quickly around, drew himself upright, and burst into hearty laughter.
“I imagine, Watson,” he said, “that you suppose I have added opium smoking to my cocaine injections and all the other little weaknesses on which you have kindly offered your medical opinions.”
“It certainly surprised me to find you there.”
“No more than finding you surprised me.”
“I was looking for a friend.”
“I was looking for an enemy.”
“An enemy of yours?”

“Yes, one of my natural enemies—or perhaps I should say my natural prey. In brief, Watson, I am engaged in a most remarkable investigation. I hoped to discover a clue in these drunkards’ incoherent ramblings, as I have done on previous occasions. Had anyone recognised me in that den, my life would not have been safe for an hour. I have used the place for my own purposes before, and the villainous Lascar who runs it has sworn revenge. At the back of the building, near the corner of Paul’s Wharf, there is a trapdoor that could tell some strange stories about what has passed through it on moonless nights.”
“What! Surely you do not mean bodies?”

“Yes, bodies, Watson. A thousand pounds for every poor soul murdered in that den would make us wealthy men. It is the foulest deathtrap along the whole riverside, and I fear Neville St. Clair has entered it never to come out again. But our carriage ought to be here.” He put his two forefingers between his teeth and gave a shrill whistle. A matching whistle answered from a distance, soon followed by rattling wheels and the clatter of horses’ hooves.
“Now, Watson,” said Holmes, as a tall dog-cart came swiftly through the gloom, its side lanterns casting two golden tunnels of light. “You will come with me, won’t you?”
“If I can be any help.”
“A reliable comrade is always helpful, and someone to record the adventure even more so. My room at The Cedars has two beds.”
“At The Cedars?”
“Yes, Mr. St. Clair’s house. I am staying there while I carry out the investigation.”
“And where is that?”
“Near Lee in Kent. There is a seven-mile drive ahead of us.”
“But I know nothing about this.”

“Naturally. You will hear everything shortly. Climb up here. Very good, John; we shall not need you. Here is half a crown. Expect me tomorrow at about eleven. Give the mare her head. Goodbye for now!”

He flicked the horse with his whip, and we sped through a seemingly endless succession of dark, deserted streets. These gradually widened until we were racing across a broad bridge with stone balustrades, the murky river moving sluggishly below. Beyond it stretched another dreary wilderness of brick and mortar. Only a policeman’s heavy, regular tread or the singing and shouting of some late party of revellers disturbed the silence. Dark clouds drifted slowly across the sky, with a star or two shining faintly through their gaps. Holmes drove without speaking, his head bowed upon his chest, apparently deep in thought. Beside him, I wondered what new investigation could be taxing his abilities so severely, but did not dare interrupt his train of thought. We had travelled several miles and were approaching the outer ring of suburban villas when he stirred, shrugged his shoulders, and lit his pipe, like a man who has decided he is taking the best course.

“You have a splendid talent for silence, Watson,” he said. “It makes you an invaluable companion. On my word, I am grateful to have someone to talk to: my own thoughts are far from pleasant. I was wondering what to say tonight when that dear little woman meets me at her door.”
“You forget that I have heard nothing about it.”

“There is just time to explain the facts before we reach Lee. The case seems absurdly simple, yet somehow I cannot find anything to work from. There is plenty of thread, certainly, but I cannot get hold of an end. Let me set it out clearly and briefly, Watson. Perhaps you will catch a glimmer where I see nothing but darkness.”
“Then go ahead.”

“Some years ago—in May 1884, to be precise—a gentleman named Neville St. Clair arrived at Lee. He appeared to have considerable means. He took a large villa, arranged its grounds very attractively, and generally lived in comfort and style. Gradually he made friends locally. In 1887 he married a local brewer’s daughter, and they now have two children. He had no profession, but held interests in several companies. Usually he went into London in the morning and returned each evening on the 5:14 from Cannon Street. Mr. St. Clair is now thirty-seven. His habits are moderate; he is a good husband, an affectionate father, and popular with everyone who knows him. I should add that, as far as we can establish, his present debts total eighty-eight pounds ten shillings, while he has two hundred and twenty pounds in the Capital and Counties Bank. There is therefore no reason to suppose financial worries have been troubling him.

“Last Monday Neville St. Clair went into town a little earlier than usual. Before leaving, he said he had two important errands and would bring his little boy a box of building bricks. By pure chance, shortly after he left that same Monday, his wife received a telegram. A small but valuable parcel she had been expecting was waiting at the Aberdeen Shipping Company’s offices. If you know your London well, you will know those offices are in Fresno Street, off Upper Swandam Lane, where you found me tonight. Mrs. St. Clair had lunch, went into the City, did some shopping, called at the company’s office, and collected her parcel. At exactly 4:35 she found herself walking along Swandam Lane towards the station. Have you followed all that?”
“That is perfectly clear.”

“You may remember how extremely hot Monday was. Mrs. St. Clair walked slowly, looking around for a cab, since she disliked the neighbourhood. As she went along Swandam Lane, she suddenly heard an exclamation or cry. To her horror, she saw her husband looking down from an open second-floor window, apparently beckoning to her. She could see his face quite clearly and described it as terribly agitated. He waved his hands frantically towards her, then disappeared from the window so abruptly that she thought some irresistible force had pulled him back from behind. Her quick feminine eye noticed one peculiar detail: although he had on a dark coat like the one in which he had left for town, he wore neither a collar nor a necktie.

“Certain that something was wrong, she rushed down the steps, for the building was the very opium den where you found me tonight. She ran through the front room and tried to climb the stairs to the first floor. At their foot, however, she encountered the Lascar scoundrel I mentioned. He forced her back and, with help from a Dane employed there as his assistant, pushed her into the street. Distracted by doubts and fears, she hurried down the lane. By exceptional good fortune, in Fresno Street she met an inspector and several constables on their way to their beats. The inspector and two officers went back with her. Despite the proprietor’s continuing resistance, they reached the room where her husband had last appeared. He was nowhere to be seen. Indeed, the entire floor contained nobody except a hideous crippled wretch who apparently lived there. Both he and the Lascar insisted that no one else had occupied the front room that afternoon. Their denials were so emphatic that the inspector hesitated. He had almost decided Mrs. St. Clair had been mistaken when she cried out, sprang towards a small deal box on the table, and tore off its lid. A shower of children’s bricks fell out. They were the toy her husband had promised to bring home.

“That discovery, together with the cripple’s obvious discomposure, convinced the inspector that something serious had happened. The rooms were searched thoroughly, and everything pointed towards a dreadful crime. The front room was a simply furnished sitting-room leading into a small bedroom that faced the rear of one of the wharves. A narrow strip of ground separates the wharf from the bedroom window. At low tide it is dry; at high tide at least four and a half feet of water cover it. The bedroom has a wide window which opens upwards from the bottom. Examination revealed traces of blood on its sill and several scattered drops on the wooden bedroom floor. Hidden behind a curtain in the sitting-room were all Neville St. Clair’s clothes except his coat. His boots, socks, hat, and watch were all there. None of the clothing showed signs of violence, and no other trace of the man could be found. Apparently he must have gone through the window, since there was no other exit. The sinister bloodstains on the sill offered little hope that he could have saved himself by swimming: the tide was at its highest when the tragedy occurred.

“Now for the villains apparently involved. The Lascar was known to have a thoroughly disreputable past. But according to Mrs. St. Clair he was at the foot of the stairs within seconds of her husband’s appearance at the window, so he could hardly have been anything more than an accomplice. He defended himself by professing complete ignorance. He claimed to know nothing of the activities of his lodger, Hugh Boone, and said he could offer no explanation whatever for the missing gentleman’s clothes being there.

“That disposes of the Lascar manager. Now consider the sinister cripple who lives on the opium den’s second floor, certainly the last person to set eyes on Neville St. Clair. His name is Hugh Boone, and anyone who frequents the City knows his hideous face. He begs professionally, though to evade police regulations he pretends to sell a few wax matches. A little way along Threadneedle Street, on the left, you may have noticed a small recess in the wall. There he sits every day, cross-legged, with his tiny stock of matches in his lap. His appearance is so pitiable that a steady sprinkling of charitable coins falls into the greasy leather cap on the pavement beside him. I have watched him more than once, long before I imagined encountering him professionally, and have been astonished by how much he collects in a short time. His looks are so striking that nobody can pass without noticing him: a mass of orange hair, a pale face marred by a terrible scar which draws the outer edge of his upper lip upwards, a bulldog chin, and piercing dark eyes that contrast oddly with his hair. All these distinguish him from ordinary beggars. So does his wit: he always has an answer ready for the jokes passers-by make at his expense. This, then, is the man we now discover lodging at the opium den, the last man to see the gentleman we are seeking.”
“But he is a cripple!” I said. “What could he have done alone against a man in the prime of life?”

“His disability consists of a limp. In every other respect he looks strong and well fed. Surely your experience as a doctor tells you, Watson, that weakness in one limb is often balanced by unusual strength in the others.”
“Please go on with the story.”

“Mrs. St. Clair fainted when she saw the blood on the window. As her presence could contribute nothing to the investigation, the police took her home in a cab. Inspector Barton, who was in charge, searched the premises very thoroughly, but discovered nothing to explain the mystery. They made one mistake by not arresting Boone immediately. He was allowed a few minutes in which he might have spoken to his friend the Lascar. That error was soon put right: he was arrested and searched, but nothing incriminating was found. There were indeed bloodstains on his right shirtsleeve. He showed them a cut near the nail of his ring finger, however, and said that was where the blood came from. He added that he had been at the window a little earlier, and that the stains there must have come from the same cut. He vehemently denied ever having seen Neville St. Clair, and swore he was as puzzled as the police by the clothes in his room. As for Mrs. St. Clair’s claim to have seen her husband at the window, he said she must be mad or dreaming. Still protesting loudly, he was taken to the police station. The inspector stayed behind, hoping the falling tide would reveal a fresh clue.

“It did, though what appeared on the mud-bank was not quite what they feared. As the water receded, it uncovered Neville St. Clair’s coat, rather than the man himself. What do you suppose they found in its pockets?”
“I cannot think.”

“No, I doubt you would guess. Pennies and half-pennies packed into every pocket: four hundred and twenty-one pennies and two hundred and seventy half-pennies. No wonder the tide had failed to carry it away. A human body would be another matter. A strong eddy runs between the wharf and the house. It seemed quite likely that the heavy coat had stayed while the naked body was sucked out into the river.”
“But you said they found all his other clothes in the room. Would he have been wearing only a coat?”

“No, but one could offer a superficially plausible explanation of the facts. Suppose Boone had pushed Neville St. Clair out through the window. Nobody could have witnessed it. What would he do next? Naturally he would realise at once that he must dispose of the incriminating clothes. He would seize the coat and begin to throw it out, then remember that it would float instead of sinking. Time is short: he has heard the struggle downstairs as the wife tried to get up, and perhaps his Lascar accomplice has already told him that the police are approaching along the street. He cannot waste a moment. He rushes to a hidden store of his earnings from begging and crams all the coins he can grab into the pockets, ensuring that the coat will sink. He throws it out. He would have done the same with the other clothing, but hears footsteps hurrying below and has barely time to shut the window before the police arrive.”
“That certainly seems possible.”

“Then, until something better occurs to us, let us use it as a working hypothesis. As I said, Boone was arrested and taken to the station. Nothing, however, could be found to suggest he had ever been in trouble before. He had been known for years as a professional beggar, but otherwise appeared to lead a quiet, blameless life. That is where matters stand. We are no nearer answering any of our questions: what brought Neville St. Clair to the opium den, what happened to him there, where he is now, and what part Hugh Boone played in his disappearance. I admit that I cannot recall another case which looked so simple at first sight and yet proved so difficult.”

As Sherlock Holmes described this extraordinary chain of events, we sped through London’s outskirts, leaving the last scattered houses behind. Soon we were rattling along between country hedges. Just as he finished, however, we passed through two straggling villages where a few windows still showed glimmers of light.

“These are the outskirts of Lee,” my companion said. “Our short drive has taken us through three English counties: from Middlesex, across a corner of Surrey, and finally into Kent. Do you see the light among those trees? That is The Cedars. Beside that lamp sits a woman whose anxious ears have already, I am almost certain, caught the sound of our horse’s hooves.”
“But why have you not been handling the case from Baker Street?” I asked.

“There are many enquiries that have to be made here. Mrs. St. Clair has very kindly given me the use of two rooms. You can be sure she will welcome my friend and colleague. I dread facing her, Watson, with no news of her husband. Here we are. Whoa, there, whoa!”

We stopped before a large villa in its own grounds. A stable-boy ran out to the horse’s head. I jumped down and followed Holmes along the short, winding gravel drive towards the house. As we approached, the door flew open. A small, fair-haired woman stood there in a light dress of mousseline de soie, with soft pink chiffon at her neck and wrists. The flood of light behind her outlined her figure. One hand rested on the door; the other was half raised in eagerness. Leaning slightly forward, her head thrust towards us, her eyes searching and her lips parted, she was a question made visible.
“Well?” she cried. “Well?” Seeing that there were two of us, she gave a hopeful cry. It turned into a groan as she saw my companion shake his head and shrug his shoulders.
“There is no good news?”
“Nothing.”
“Nothing bad?”
“No.”
“Thank God for that. Come inside, though. You must be exhausted after such a long day.”
“This is my friend, Dr. Watson. He has given me invaluable help on several cases. A fortunate chance has allowed me to bring him here and enlist his assistance in this investigation.”
“I am very glad to meet you,” she said, warmly clasping my hand. “I am sure you will forgive any shortcomings in our hospitality when you consider the sudden blow that has fallen upon us.”

“My dear madam,” I replied, “I am an old soldier, accustomed to rough conditions. Even if I were not, I should see that no apology was necessary. I shall be very happy if I can help either you or my friend here.”

“Now, Mr. Sherlock Holmes,” she said as we entered a brightly lit dining-room, where a cold supper stood ready on the table, “I want to ask you one or two direct questions. Please give me equally direct answers.”
“Of course, madam.”
“Do not spare my feelings. I am neither hysterical nor inclined to faint. I simply want to hear your true, honest opinion.”
“About what, exactly?”
“Deep in your heart, do you believe Neville is still alive?”
The question seemed to embarrass Sherlock Holmes. “Speak frankly!” she insisted. Standing on the rug, she looked searchingly down at him as he leaned back in a wicker chair.
“To be frank, madam, I do not.”
“You believe that he is dead?”
“I do.”
“Was he murdered?”
“I would not say that. Possibly.”
“And what day do you believe he died?”
“It was Monday.”
“Then perhaps, Mr. Holmes, you would kindly explain how I came to receive a letter from him today.”
Sherlock Holmes leaped from his chair as though struck by an electric shock.
“What!” he bellowed.
“Yes, today.” Smiling, she held a small piece of paper up in the air.
“May I look at it?”
“Of course.”

In his eagerness he seized it from her, flattened it on the table, drew the lamp closer, and studied it intently. I rose from my chair and looked over his shoulder. The envelope was made of very coarse paper and bore a Gravesend postmark dated that very day—or rather the previous day, since midnight was now well behind us.
“Rough handwriting,” Holmes murmured. “Surely your husband did not write this, madam?”
“No, but he wrote what is inside.”
“I can also see that the person who addressed the envelope had to ask someone for the address.”
“How do you know that?”

“Look: the ink of the name is deep black, having dried naturally. The rest is greyish, showing that blotting-paper was used. If the whole had been written at once and then blotted, none of it would be so black. The writer put down the name, then paused before adding the address. That can only mean he did not know it. A small detail, certainly, but nothing matters more than small details. Now let us examine the letter. Ah! Something else was enclosed!”
“Yes, a ring. It was his signet-ring.”
“And you are certain this is your husband’s handwriting?”
“One style of his handwriting.”
“One style?”
“The way he writes in a hurry. It is very different from his ordinary hand, but I recognise it well.”

“‘My dearest, do not be afraid. Everything will turn out well. There has been a great mistake, which may take a little time to put right. Wait patiently.—NEVILLE.’ Pencil on a book’s flyleaf, octavo size, without a watermark. Hmm! Posted today at Gravesend by a man with a dirty thumb. Ah! Unless I am badly mistaken, the person who moistened the envelope’s flap had been chewing tobacco. And you have no doubts about this being your husband’s writing, madam?”
“None at all. Neville wrote those words.”
“And someone posted them today at Gravesend. Well, Mrs. St. Clair, things look brighter, though I would not yet say the danger has passed.”
“But surely he must be alive, Mr. Holmes.”
“Unless this is a skilful forgery intended to mislead us. The ring itself proves nothing, after all. Someone may have taken it from him.”
“No, no! It is his writing, his very own!”
“Very well. But he could have written it on Monday, and it was only posted today.”
“That could be so.”
“In that case, much could have happened since.”

“Oh, do not take away my hope, Mr. Holmes. I know he is safe. We are so closely in sympathy that I would know if anything dreadful happened to him. On the last day I saw him, he cut himself in the bedroom. I was in the dining-room, yet I rushed upstairs at once, absolutely certain something had happened. Could I sense so small a thing and still be unaware of his death?”

“I have seen enough to know that a woman’s intuition can be worth more than an analytical thinker’s conclusions. This letter certainly gives you strong evidence to support your belief. But if your husband is alive and able to write to you, why does he stay away?”
“I have no idea. It is inconceivable.”
“Did he say anything on Monday before he left you?”
“No.”
“And seeing him in Swandam Lane came as a surprise?”
“A very great surprise.”
“Was that window open?”
“Yes.”
“So he could have called out to you?”
“He could have.”
“But, as I understand it, his cry contained no words?”
“Yes.”
“You took it as a call for help?”
“Yes. He was waving his hands.”
“It could, though, have been a cry of surprise. The astonishment of seeing you unexpectedly might have made him throw up his hands?”
“That is possible.”
“And you believed someone pulled him back?”
“He vanished so abruptly.”
“Perhaps he jumped back. You saw nobody else in the room, did you?”
“No. But that horrible man admitted he had been there, and the Lascar stood at the bottom of the stairs.”
“Quite. As far as you could tell, your husband was wearing his usual clothes?”
“Except for his collar and tie. I clearly saw his bare throat.”
“Had he ever mentioned Swandam Lane to you?”
“Never.”
“Had you ever seen any indication that he used opium?”
“Never.”
“Thank you, Mrs. St. Clair. Those were the main points on which I needed absolute clarity. Now we should have a little supper and go to bed. Tomorrow may be a very busy day.”

We had been given a large, comfortable room with two beds. Exhausted by the night’s adventures, I was soon under the sheets. Sherlock Holmes, however, could go for days—even a week—without rest when an unsolved problem occupied his mind. He would turn it over, rearrange the facts, and examine it from every angle until he either understood it or satisfied himself that his information was inadequate. I soon realised he was preparing to remain awake all night. He removed his coat and waistcoat, put on a loose blue dressing-gown, and wandered about gathering pillows from his bed and cushions from the sofa and armchairs. He piled these into a kind of Eastern divan and settled on it cross-legged, with an ounce of shag tobacco and a box of matches in front of him. In the lamplight I could see him sitting motionless and silent, an old briar pipe between his lips, his eyes fixed unseeingly on a corner of the ceiling. Blue smoke rose around him, and the light picked out his firm, aquiline features. He was sitting like that when I fell asleep. He was still there when a sudden exclamation woke me and I found summer sunshine pouring into the room. The pipe remained between his lips and smoke still curled upwards. A dense tobacco haze filled the room, but the heap of shag I had seen the night before had entirely disappeared.
“Are you awake, Watson?” he asked.
“Yes.”
“Would you enjoy a morning drive?”
“Certainly.”

“Then get dressed. Nobody is up yet, but I know where the stable-boy sleeps. We can soon have the carriage ready.” He chuckled as he spoke, his eyes sparkling. He seemed quite a different man from the sombre thinker of the night before.
I checked my watch while dressing. No wonder the household was still asleep: it was twenty-five past four. I had scarcely finished when Holmes returned to say that the boy was harnessing the horse.

“I want to test a small theory,” he said, pulling on his boots. “Watson, I believe you are standing before one of the greatest fools in Europe. I deserve to be kicked all the way from here to Charing Cross. Still, I think I have found the key to the mystery.”
“And where might that be?” I asked, smiling.

“In the bathroom,” he replied. Seeing my disbelief, he added, “Yes, I mean it. I have just been there, taken it away, and put it in this Gladstone bag. Come along, my boy. Let us see whether it fits the lock.”

As quietly as we could, we went downstairs and out into the bright morning sun. The horse and carriage stood in the road, with the half-dressed stable-boy waiting at the horse’s head. We climbed in and sped along the London Road. A few country carts were already carrying vegetables into the capital, but the villas on either side were as silent and lifeless as a city in a dream.
“In some ways this has been an unusual case,” Holmes said, flicking the horse into a gallop. “I admit I have been as blind as a mole. But learning wisdom late is better than never learning it.”

As we drove through the streets on the Surrey side, the earliest risers were just beginning to peer sleepily from their windows. We followed Waterloo Bridge Road, crossed the river, hurried up Wellington Street, and turned sharply right into Bow Street. The police knew Sherlock Holmes well, and both constables at the entrance saluted him. One took the horse’s head while the other showed us inside.
“Who is in charge here?” Holmes asked.
